title: Class D, E, and G Airspace — Entry, Communications, and Boundaries

required_knowledge_points.title: Class D Airspace — Tower Communication and the Part-Time Surprise
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'The tower is closed. What airspace are you operating in?' When a Class D tower closes, the airspace reverts to Class E or Class G depending on what the Chart Supplement specifies — not a predictable default. This is one of the most tested operational transitions on the checkride.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Class D airspace surrounds airports with operating control towers not meeting Class C volume threshold. Dimensions: typically 4 NM radius, surface to 2,500 feet AGL. Depicted: dashed blue circle on sectional charts. Entry requirements: two-way radio communication prior to entry (callsign acknowledgment required — not explicit clearance). Required visibility: 3 SM, 500 below / 1,000 above / 2,000 horizontal. Part-time Class D: when the tower closes, the airspace reverts. The Chart Supplement specifies what it becomes after hours — typically Class E if instrument approaches are authorized, Class G if not. Pilots must check the Chart Supplement — not the sectional — for after-hours designation.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Class D Airspace — Core Facts
- Surrounds airports with **operating control towers** (not meeting Class C volume)
- Dimensions: typically **4 NM radius**, surface to **2,500 feet AGL**
- Depicted: **dashed blue circle** on sectional charts

### Entry Requirements
- **Two-way radio communication** established before entering
- ATC must acknowledge your **callsign** — 'N123AB, standby' = ✅ sufficient
- 'Aircraft in the pattern, standby' (no callsign) = ❌ **NOT sufficient**
- **No Mode C transponder** specifically required (beyond general airspace rules)

### VFR Weather Minimums
- **3 SM** visibility
- **500 below / 1,000 above / 2,000 horizontal** cloud separation

### Part-Time Class D — Tower Closure
| After Hours | What Airspace Becomes | Source to Check |
|---|---|---|
| IAP approaches authorized | **Class E** from the surface | **Chart Supplement** (not the sectional) |
| No IAP approaches | **Class G** | Chart Supplement |

> **Checkride Trap:** The sectional still shows the dashed blue Class D circle after the tower closes — but the airspace has legally changed. Always check the **Chart Supplement** for after-hours designation, never assume

required_knowledge_points.title: Class E Airspace — The Default Controlled Airspace Nobody Fully Understands
required_knowledge_points.why: The most misunderstood airspace class: Class E has no communications requirement for VFR flight, but it is controlled airspace with IFR separation and weather minimums that change based on altitude. The DPE tests whether the applicant knows Class E weather minimums change at 10,000 MSL — and why.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Class E: the catch-all controlled airspace — all controlled airspace not designated A, B, C, or D. Class E begins at: (1) 1,200 feet AGL over most of the U.S. (magenta shading fades toward white — the fade marks the E floor at 1,200 AGL). (2) 700 feet AGL in transition areas near airports with instrument approaches (solid magenta boundary). (3) Surface extensions: dashed magenta line = Class E from the surface (untowered airports with instrument approaches). Entry requirements: NONE for VFR — no radio call, no transponder beyond general rules. VFR weather minimums: (a) Below 10,000 MSL: 3 SM, 500 below / 1,000 above / 2,000 horizontal. (b) At or above 10,000 MSL: 5 SM, 1,000 below / 1,000 above / 1 SM horizontal. The 10,000 MSL shift is because higher-altitude IFR aircraft operate at higher speeds — greater visual buffer needed for see-and-avoid.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Class E — What It Is
- **Catch-all controlled airspace** — all controlled airspace not designated A, B, C, or D
- **No communications requirement** for VFR flight
- **No ATC contact** needed to be in Class E legally

### Where Class E Begins
| Symbology | Class E Floor |
|---|---|
| Magenta **fades** to white (no boundary) | **1,200 AGL** (most of the U.S.) |
| **Solid magenta** boundary line (transition area) | **700 AGL** near airports with instrument approaches |
| **Dashed magenta** boundary line | **Surface** — Class E surface extension for IFR approach protection |

### VFR Weather Minimums in Class E
| Altitude | Visibility | Cloud Separation |
|---|---|---|
| **Below 10,000 MSL** | 3 SM | 500 below / 1,000 above / 2,000 horizontal |
| **At or above 10,000 MSL** | **5 SM** | **1,000 below / 1,000 above / 1 SM horizontal** |

> Minimums jump at 10,000 MSL because higher-altitude aircraft operate at higher speeds — greater visual buffer is required for effective see-and-avoid

required_knowledge_points.title: Class G Airspace — The Wild West of Uncontrolled Airspace
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'What are the VFR weather minimums at night in Class G airspace at 800 feet AGL?' Answer: 3 SM and clear of clouds. The trap: daytime minimums in Class G below 1,200 AGL are 1 SM and clear of clouds — but nighttime jumps to 3 SM regardless of altitude.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Class G: uncontrolled airspace — no ATC services, no communication requirement, no ATC facility. Class G exists from the surface to the base of Class E (typically 700 or 1,200 AGL). No entry requirements. VFR weather minimums in Class G: (a) Day, at or below 1,200 AGL: 1 SM, clear of clouds. (b) Day, above 1,200 AGL but below 10,000 MSL: 1 SM, 500 below / 1,000 above / 2,000 horizontal. (c) Night, at or below 1,200 AGL: 3 SM, clear of clouds. (d) Night, above 1,200 AGL but below 10,000 MSL: 3 SM, 500 below / 1,000 above / 2,000 horizontal. Key: nighttime Class G minimum jumps to 3 SM at all altitudes. Rationale: at night, physiological limitations reduce see-and-avoid capability that makes 1 SM daytime minimums viable.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Class G — What It Is
- **Uncontrolled airspace** — no ATC services, no communication requirement
- Exists from the **surface** to the **base of Class E** (typically 700 or 1,200 AGL)
- **No entry requirements** — VFR pilots may operate freely within weather minimums

### VFR Weather Minimums in Class G — Full Table
| Altitude | Time | Visibility | Cloud Separation |
|---|---|---|---|
| At or below **1,200 AGL** | **Day** | **1 SM** | **Clear of clouds** |
| At or below **1,200 AGL** | **Night** | **3 SM** | **Clear of clouds** |
| Above 1,200 AGL, below 10,000 MSL | **Day** | 1 SM | 500 below / 1,000 above / 2,000 horizontal |
| Above 1,200 AGL, below 10,000 MSL | **Night** | **3 SM** | 500 below / 1,000 above / 2,000 horizontal |

### Why the Night Minimums Increase
- At night, **human vision** cannot reliably detect traffic, terrain, and obstacles at 1 SM
- Night minimum jumps to **3 SM at ALL Class G altitudes** — even below 1,200 AGL

> **Checkride Trap:** Daytime Class G below 1,200 AGL = only **1 SM**. Night Class G same altitude = **3 SM**. Mixing up day/night G minimums is one of the most common oral exam failures

required_knowledge_points.title: Reading the Sectional — Airspace Boundaries by Color and Symbol
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE places a sectional on the table and points to a location: 'What airspace is this, and what are the weather minimums?' This requires reading the chart visually. Applicants who can recite minimums but cannot identify airspace class from chart symbols fail this part of the oral.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Sectional chart airspace symbology: (1) Solid blue circle — Class B shelves with ceiling/floor labels. (2) Solid blue segmented circle — Class C 5 NM and 10 NM rings. (3) Dashed blue circle — Class D, typically 4 NM radius. (4) Dashed magenta boundary — Class E surface extension (untowered airports with instrument approaches). (5) Solid magenta shading/fading — Class E floor transitions. Where magenta fades (toward white), Class E begins at 700 AGL. Beyond the fade (no shading), Class E begins at 1,200 AGL. (6) No symbology for Class G — if no airspace class is depicted and you are below the E floor, you are in Class G. Airport icons: Blue airport symbol = towered (Class B/C/D). Magenta airport symbol = untowered (Class E or G).
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Sectional Chart Airspace Symbology — Quick Reference

| Symbol | Airspace Class |
|---|---|
| **Solid blue lines** with ceiling/floor labels | **Class B** shelves |
| **Solid blue segmented circles** (two rings) | **Class C** — 5 NM and 10 NM rings |
| **Dashed blue circle** | **Class D** — typically 4 NM radius |
| **Dashed magenta boundary** | **Class E surface extension** — IFR approach protection, untowered |
| **Solid magenta shading** fading to white | **Class E at 700 AGL** (transition area) |
| **No magenta shading** (white/terrain tones) | **Class E at 1,200 AGL** — beyond the fade |
| **No depiction at all** (below E floor) | **Class G** |

### Airport Icon Colors
| Icon Color | Tower Status | Airspace |
|---|---|---|
| **Blue** airport symbol | **Towered** | Class B, C, or D |
| **Magenta** airport symbol | **Untowered** | Class E or G |

> A magenta airport inside a **dashed magenta boundary** = untowered airport in **Class E from the surface** — controlled airspace minimums apply even without a tower

lesson_overview:
## Class D, E, and G Airspace — The Roads Less Traveled (But No Less Regulated)

The airspace below the big airports is where most training flights happen. It's also where most pilots make airspace mistakes. Class D, E, and G cover the vast majority of the country's airspace — including uncontrolled airports that feel casual but sometimes hide regulatory gotchas.

**Class D: the tower airport.** Class D typically forms a 4 NM radius circle, from the surface to 2,500 AGL. It exists wherever there's an operating control tower that doesn't qualify for Class C. The key word is *operating* — Class D is only Class D when the tower is open. Entry requirement: two-way radio communication established before entering. 'N123AB, standby' = sufficient. 'Aircraft in the pattern, standby' without callsign = NOT sufficient.

**The Class D after-hours question.** What happens when the Class D tower closes? The sectional still shows the dashed blue circle — but the airspace itself reverts to something specified in the Chart Supplement. Some airports revert to Class E (if there are instrument approaches protecting the surface). Others revert to Class G. Do not guess — look it up in the Chart Supplement before every flight to a part-time Class D airport.

**Class E: controlled but wide open to VFR.** Class E is the largest airspace classification in the U.S. by volume. No radio requirement, no ATC contact needed to be in Class E VFR. Class E typically begins at 1,200 AGL but drops to 700 AGL in transition areas (solid magenta boundary). A dashed magenta line = Class E from the surface. The critical altitude transition: below 10,000 MSL, VFR minimums are 3 SM and 500/1,000/2,000. At or above 10,000 MSL, minimums jump to 5 SM and 1,000/1,000/1 SM.

**Class G: uncontrolled and underappreciated.** Class G fills the gap from the surface to the floor of Class E. The extremely low VFR minimums reflect remote, low-traffic areas: daytime at or below 1,200 AGL requires only 1 SM and clear of clouds. At night: 3 SM. Nighttime physiological limitations of human vision eliminate the see-and-avoid capability that makes 1-mile daytime minimums viable.

**Reading the sectional from memory.** Solid blue = Class B. Blue segmented circles = Class C. Dashed blue = Class D. Dashed magenta = Class E surface. Solid magenta fades = Class E at 700 AGL. No marking + below E floor = Class G. Blue airport icon = tower. Magenta airport icon = untowered.

**The checkride trap:** The DPE closes the sectional and asks: 'You're at an untowered airport with a dashed magenta line around it. The ceiling is 800 feet. What airspace and what are the minimums?' Answer: Class E from the surface, 3 SM visibility minimum, standard cloud separation. The dashed magenta is not a tower — it's a protection boundary for instrument approaches. No comm required but Class E minimums apply.
